headline: High: oh-my-openagent can exfiltrate project code and auth data while LightZero is a non-writing game agent, creating default data-leak and compliance risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightZero has no filesystem or network surfaces, so it cannot be directly hijacked. However, oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and reads project files, so if LightZero outputs are copied into shared files or prompts, injected instructions could be parsed. The pathway is interaction-based, not impossible.
conditions: IF the pair is bridged by a shared file, clipboard, or prompt relay
IF oh-my-openagent parses LightZero-generated text as instructions
mitigations: Disable any shared clipboard or file relay between the agents
Require a human review step before copying LightZero output into oh-my-openagent
Strip markdown/code fences from transferred text
Use a dedicated scratch file with read-only access for LightZero outputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all inter-agent text

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightZero touches no data classes and has no egress, but oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data, and has broad network egress. If both share a workspace or files, sensitive content can flow from B to external services by default. The blast radius includes code and credentials, so this is high.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent is pointed at a workspace containing secrets or auth prompts
IF shared files from LightZero are opened by oh-my-openagent
mitigations: Remove secrets from any shared workspace before running oh-my-openagent
Disable network egress for oh-my-openagent during joint runs
Use separate directories for each agent
Rotate any provider auth data exposed in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightZero cannot write files, modify git, or use network, so it cannot conflict on mutable resources. oh-my-openagent can spawn subprocesses and has broad egress, but without overlapping write surfaces there is no meaningful write-write contention. The pair is mostly read-only from LightZero's side.
conditions: IF LightZero is extended with write or git capabilities
IF both agents are given the same mutable directory
mitigations: Keep LightZero read-only
Assign separate working directories
Avoid concurrent edits to the same repo
Use file locks for any shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightZero is a game-playing agent that can generate outputs later consumed by oh-my-openagent, which can act on project files and external APIs. If oh-my-openagent treats LightZero output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect actions or code changes. The interaction is plausible in default agent workflows, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent uses LightZero output as an input artifact
IF no verification step is inserted before downstream actions
mitigations: Require explicit verification before acting on LightZero output
Limit LightZero output to advisory text only
Log and diff any downstream changes
Use a second reviewer for actions derived from LightZero
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: LightZero is open-source game-playing software with no touched data classes, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts, session history, project code, and telemetry with broad egress. That creates a compliance mismatch around retention and third-party transmission if shared data includes sensitive project material. The other agent is not cited for residency because none is specified.
conditions: IF shared inputs include regulated or confidential project data
IF oh-my-openagent uploads that data to third-party services
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from shared runs
Review telemetry and retention settings
Separate auth prompts from project workspaces
Document data handling for joint workflows
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
